one_liner: Zig HTTP/1.1 server library on epoll/kqueue; ties actix-web on hello-world req/s, leading ~5% only at 512 connections.
what_it_does: http.zig (module name httpz) is an HTTP/1.1 server written in Zig that does not use std.http.Server, which its README calls 'very slow' and says 'assumes well-behaved clients'. You call httpz.Server(H).init(io, allocator, config, handler), register routes such as router.get("/api/user/:id", action, .{}), and write actions as fn(req: *httpz.Request, res: *httpz.Response) !void; an optional handler type H can share app state and override dispatch, notFound, uncaughtError, or take over request handling entirely. It bundles a router (params, globs, groups), middleware (built-in CORS), query/form/multipart/JSON parsing, lazy body reads, chunked request bodies, SSE, WebSocket upgrade via websocket.zig, Prometheus-style metrics and a unit-test helper; the JetZig and Tokamak frameworks are built on it. It is not a drop-in for actix-web: different language, API and concurrency model.
how_it_is_fast: N worker threads each run their own epoll (Linux) or kqueue (BSD/macOS) loop over one shared non-blocking listener (the epoll registration uses EPOLLEXCLUSIVE to limit thundering-herd wakeups) and parse requests incrementally into a pre-allocated per-connection Request.State buffer, so bytes that trickle in are not re-parsed. Parsed requests are queued, in batches of up to 16 to cut locking, to a separate thread pool that runs the action and writes the response with blocking writev, then hands the connection back to its worker through a handover list. Per-request memory comes from a FallbackAllocator: a thread-local fixed buffer (thread_pool.buffer_size) first, then the connection's retained arena, plus per-worker pools of large buffers, so the hot path rarely reaches the general-purpose allocator. The parser compares 4-byte words as u32 to match methods and the 'HTTP/1.x' version, and lower-cases header names in place.
when_to_use: Your service is already in Zig and needs an HTTP/1.1 API server. In the 2026-09-24 run httpz reached 146k-171k req/s, while zzz, the other Zig framework in that run, reached 57k-69k req/s (derived from page data).
Deployment behind a reverse proxy such as nginx that terminates TLS and tolerates non-compliant upstreams. The README designs for this and recommends proxy-side timeouts.

Keep-alive REST/JSON traffic with small requests at high connection counts, where median latency matters. httpz's p50 was lower than actix-web's at every level: 0.29/1.22/2.52 ms vs 0.35/1.52/3.13 ms at c=64/256/512 (derived from page data).

Actions that make blocking calls, such as a pg.zig pool query. Actions run on a thread pool (default 32 threads) sized separately from the epoll workers, so a blocking action does not stall the event loop.
You want a bounded memory footprint you can size up front. The README gives a minimum-memory formula from thread_pool, workers and request buffer settings.
when_not_to_use: Tail latency matters. In the same run httpz's p99 was 3.48/5.58/9.13 ms vs actix-web's 0.39/1.58/3.22 ms at c=64/256/512, 2.8x-8.8x higher, and its c=64 throughput was 18% lower (derived from page data).
You need TLS, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 in-process. The parser accepts only HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1, and the owner said in issue #148 he would add TLS only if Zig's std gains a tls.Server.

Clients connect directly without a proxy. The README says httpz 'may never be fully HTTP/1.1 compliant' (e.g. no Date header), timeouts are effectively disabled by default, and non-epoll/kqueue platforms such as Windows use a thread-per-connection blocking mode the README calls easy to DoS.

You need a stable toolchain or proven concurrency. master targets Zig 0.16.0 and the README calls this port 'not well tested' and 'experimental'. Issue #125, open since 2025-05, reports ThreadSanitizer races and a 'switch on corrupt value' panic under 100 concurrent slow requests on an older version; a later comment traces a crash to epoll returning an fd closed in the previous batch.
Windows production use. Open issues report a service being killed (#182) and cross-thread websocket writes hanging in blocking mode (#74), and the owner says he cannot reproduce Windows problems.

integration.form: module (Zig package added with zig fetch and build.zig.zon; compiled from source)
integration.dependencies: metrics.zig and websocket.zig (Zig packages pinned in build.zig.zon); links libc (link_libc = true)
integration.min_toolchain: Zig 0.16.0 on master; zig-0.15 branch for Zig 0.15; dev branch tracks Zig master
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll) and BSD/macOS (kqueue) in non-blocking mode; everything else, notably Windows, runs a thread-per-connection blocking mode
integration.thread_safety: Actions run concurrently on the thread pool. The handler instance passed to Server(H).init is shared by all concurrent requests, so its state must be thread-safe; put per-request data in a context built in dispatch. Request and Response objects are per request.

gotchas: res.body and res.header name/value slices must stay valid until the response is sent after the action returns. Allocate them from res.arena, or use res.headerOpts with dupe_name/dupe_value.

Limits drop data silently: headers beyond request.max_header_count (32), route params beyond max_param_count (10) and query params beyond max_query_count (32) are ignored. formData()/multiFormData() return nothing useful until max_form_count/max_multiform_count are set above their default of 0. All request headers must fit in request.buffer_size (4 KB default), else the request is rejected.

Chunked request bodies are always buffered fully in memory and ignore lazy_read_size (owner, issue #170). multiFormData() rewrites escaped field names inside the raw body in place, and each SSE stream from startEventStream runs on its own new thread.

Defaults are 1 epoll worker and 32 pool threads (config.zig); the benchmark set both to the CPU count, so tune workers.count before comparing. The router does not backtrack: with '/:any/users' and '/hello/users/test' registered, '/hello/users' matches nothing, and routes must be lowercase (README).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick httpz when the application is in Zig and you want a full-featured server library (router, middleware, WebSocket, test helpers) rather than a bare parser. If you are not tied to Zig, fulmine.js (204k), may_minihttp (194k), ohkami-nio (182k) and httpbeast (176k) all beat httpz's 171k req/s at c=512 in the same run, and fulmine.js, may_minihttp and ohkami-nio also had lower p99 (derived from page data).
verified_claims_summary: In the-benchmarker/web-frameworks run of 2026-09-24 (develop, commit f673364), httpz commit 52eb187 built with Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast averaged 146k/168k/171k req/s over three hello-world routes at 64/256/512 closed-loop keep-alive connections vs actix-web 4.8 (Rust 1.98, release, LTO) at 179k/168k/163k, i.e. 0.82x/1.00x/1.05x, with the server pinned to 4 cores of an undisclosed 16-thread x86_64 Linux host. The 2026-09-20 snapshot of the same httpz commit under an older load method showed 1.49x-1.64x, so the ratio depends on how the suite measures, not on httpz changes.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-26, 1.6k stars) and MIT-licensed, consumed as a Zig package; the Zig 0.16 port on master is self-described as experimental, and older Zig versions live on zig-X.YY branches.
